e.etymology: A name with several unrelated sources: a Finnish name, a variant of Airi; a Latvian name first recorded in 1934; and a Japanese girl's name.
From Hebrew oren, pine tree. Oren appears briefly in 1 Chronicles as a son of Jerahmeel; the name was used in 19th-century America and is common in modern Israel.
A spelling of Kane, an Irish surname from O Cathain, descendant of Cathan, a name built on cath, battle. The surname Kaine can also be a variant of Coyne or Cohen.

assoc.t: sounds like Cain, who killed his brother Abel in Genesis
Tim Kaine, Virginia senator and 2016 VP nominee

e.note: Sounds the same as Cain, the Bible's first murderer.

e.etymology: From Hebrew Benayahu, Yahweh has built. In the Bible, Benaiah son of Jehoiada is one of David's mighty men, who killed a lion in a pit on a snowy day and later led Solomon's army.

e.meaning: from Elias, my God is Yahweh
e.etymology: A spelling of Elliott, a surname from a medieval French pet form of Elias, the Greek form of Elijah, my God is Yahweh. This spelling recalls the writers T. S. Eliot and George Eliot.
namesakes: T. S. Eliot (poet of The Waste Land)
Eliot Ness (Prohibition agent who pursued Al Capone)
George Eliot (pen name of novelist Mary Ann Evans)

e.etymology: The Spanish, Italian, Portuguese and Romanian form of Christina, from Latin Christiana, a follower of Christ.
namesakes: Cristina Yang (Sandra Oh's surgeon on Grey's Anatomy)

e.etymology: From a surname taken from a place in Normandy, Old French la mare, the pool. It became a first name in the American South, honoring figures such as Texas president Mirabeau B. Lamar.
A spelling of Zachary, the English form of Zacharias, from Hebrew Zekharyah, Yahweh has remembered.
From Norman French Archambault, from Germanic erkan (genuine, precious) and bald (bold). It became a favorite in Scotland, where it also stood in for the Gaelic name Gillespie.
A recent American name, most likely a short feminine take on Ryan or a trimmed form of Riya and Raya. Rya is also the Swedish word for a traditional shaggy wool rug.
A phonetic spelling of Malachi, from Hebrew Malakhi, my messenger, the last of the twelve minor prophets. Malaki is also the Hawaiian form of the name.
The Arabic form of Zechariah, from Hebrew Zekharyah, Yahweh has remembered. In the Quran, Zakariya is a prophet, the father of Yahya (John the Baptist) and guardian of Mary.
A form of Aslan, the Turkish word for lion, long used as a name across the Muslim world. This spelling is common in Pakistan and Malaysia.
e.note: Sounds the same as Aslan, the lion of C.S. Lewis's Chronicles of Narnia.

e.etymology: From French Aimée, beloved, the past participle of aimer, to love, and the source of the English name Amy. Americans usually write it without the accent.
namesakes: Aimee Lou Wood (Sex Education and The White Lotus actress)
Aimee Semple McPherson (1920s Los Angeles evangelist)

e.meaning: seashore, the land beside the sea
e.etymology: The English word for the shoreline, from Old French coste and Latin costa, rib or side. It is a recent nature name in the line of Ocean, Reef and Bay.

assoc.t: Coast bar soap and body wash

e.etymology: A spelling of Leila, from Arabic Layla, night. The name is famous from the old love story of Layla and Majnun and entered English through 19th-century literature.
A modern American name, either a feminine respelling of the surname Harlan or a blend of Harley and the -lyn ending.
An Americanized spelling of Kaiser, the German word for emperor, which descends from the Roman title Caesar. Kyzer also exists as an American surname.
e.note: Sounds identical to Kaiser, the title of Germany's emperors and the name of the Kaiser Permanente health system.

e.etymology: A spelling of Everett, an English surname from the Germanic name Everard: eber, wild boar, plus hard, brave or strong. The -ette spelling was most used in the 1910s.
A fanciful spelling of Xavier, from the Basque place name Etxeberria, new house. Xavier became a first name in honor of the 16th-century Jesuit missionary Saint Francis Xavier.
From the Latin saint's name Maximus, greatest. Maxim is the usual form in Russian, Ukrainian and Czech, matching French Maxime and Italian Massimo.

assoc.t: maxim, the English word for a short rule or saying
Maxim gun, the first automatic machine gun

e.note: Shares its name with the men's magazine Maxim; maxim is also an English word for a saying.

e.etymology: A Yiddish and Hebrew short form of Yeshaya, the Hebrew original of Isaiah, meaning God is salvation. It is a familiar boys' name in Orthodox Jewish families.

e.meaning: from Courtenay, a Norman place name
e.etymology: From the aristocratic Norman surname Courtenay, taken from places in Normandy named for a Roman called Curtenus, from Latin curtus, short. First a men's name, it turned mostly female in the 20th century.
namesakes: Courtney Love (singer of the band Hole)

e.etymology: Probably an anglicized form of the name of the 6th-century Irish saint Ailbe, also called Saint Elvis; its ultimate origin is uncertain. Elvis Presley, who shared it with his father Vernon Elvis Presley, made it world famous.
namesakes: Elvis Presley (the King of Rock and Roll)

assoc.t: Elvis Presley, the King of Rock and Roll

e.note: Nearly everyone will think of Elvis Presley first.

e.meaning: from the River Shannon, Ireland's longest river
e.etymology: From Irish Sionainn, the River Shannon, whose name is linked to an old word for wisdom. It was first given as a first name in the United States in the early 20th century and only later in Ireland.
namesakes: Shannon Sharpe (NFL Hall of Famer and sports commentator)

e.etymology: Either an anglicized form of Irish Mícheál and Scottish Gaelic Mìcheal, or simply a common respelling of Michael. All go back to Hebrew Mikha'el, who is like God?, the name of the archangel.
e.note: Usually read as a misspelling of Michael, so expect it to be corrected on forms and in school.

e.meaning: deep gorge cut by a river
e.etymology: The English word for a deep river gorge, borrowed in the American West from Spanish cañón, tube or gorge. It has been used as a first name since the late 20th century.
A respelling of Kinsley, an English surname and Yorkshire place name usually explained as Old English cyne, royal, plus leah, a woodland clearing or meadow.
A modern American spelling of Vada or Veda that makes the VAY-duh pronunciation plain. Vada became known through Vada Sultenfuss, the girl in the 1991 film My Girl.
The feminine form of Peter, from Greek petra, rock. It came into regular use in the 19th century and is far more common in central and northern Europe than in the US.

assoc.t: Petra, the ancient rock-cut city in Jordan
Petra, Christian rock band of the 1970s to 2000s

e.etymology: A fanciful spelling of Jackson, an English surname meaning son of Jack. Jack began as a medieval pet form of John.
A short form of Krishna, from Sanskrit krishna, dark or black. Krishna is one of the most widely worshipped Hindu gods, an avatar of Vishnu.
